title: Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenised Deposits and CBDCs
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and central bankers to assess stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs, and their risks to payments and financial stability.
intro: This training programme equips supervisors and central bank staff to understand, regulate and oversee new forms of digital money: assessing stablecoin issuers and reserves, tokenised deposits and CBDC design, and their implications for payments and financial stability.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors and central bankers a clear, technology-neutral understanding of how stablecoins, tokenised deposits and central bank digital currencies work, and of the risks they pose to consumers, payment systems and monetary and financial stability. Participants leave able to assess issuers' reserves, redemption and resilience, challenge business models and contribute to the authority's policy on digital money.
sections.What It Covers: The forms of digital money and the singleness of money, stablecoin design and business models, authorisation and prudential requirements, reserves, redemption and run risk, tokenised deposits, retail and wholesale CBDCs, payments and financial stability, financial crime and consumer protection, cross-border interoperability, and supervising digital money issuers.
Intended Audience: Supervisors responsible for e-money, payment, crypto-asset and banking firms engaging with digital money
Central bank staff in payments, market infrastructure, financial stability and monetary policy functions
Policy, legal and innovation teams shaping the authority's approach to stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs
Learning Objectives: Explain how stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs differ in design, legal claim and risk
Assess stablecoin reserve composition, custody, redemption arrangements and run risk
Evaluate authorisation, prudential and conduct requirements for issuers of digital money
Analyse the implications of digital money for payment systems, bank funding, monetary sovereignty and financial stability
Identify financial crime and consumer protection risks and the supervisory responses to them
Design a supervisory and policy approach to digital money issuers and arrangements
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with case studies, red flags and supervisory question exercises, closing with a de-pegging scenario workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored for supervisory or central bank audiences.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: A basic understanding of crypto-assets and blockchain is helpful, for example from a fundamentals course. Familiarity with payments or banking supervision is useful but not essential.
Core Reading: BIS, Annual Economic Report 2023, Chapter III: Blueprint for the Future Monetary System
FSB, High-level Recommendations for the Regulation, Supervision and Oversight of Global Stablecoin Arrangements (2023)
CPMI-IOSCO, Application of the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures to Stablecoin Arrangements (2022)
BIS and central banks, Central Bank Digital Currencies: Foundational Principles and Core Features (2020)

modules.title: The Landscape of Digital Money
modules.summary: A map of public and private money in digital form, the role of trust and settlement in money, and why the singleness of money matters to supervisors and central banks.
objectives: Distinguish central bank money, commercial bank money, e-money and stablecoins
Explain the singleness of money and why it underpins trust in payments
Identify the drivers of private and public innovation in digital money
syllabus: The two-tier monetary system and settlement in central bank money
E-money, stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs compared
Legal claims: on whom, for what and when
BIS, CPMI and FSB perspectives on the future monetary system

modules.title: Stablecoin Design and Business Models
modules.summary: How stablecoins are structured, issued, distributed and redeemed, the economics of issuers, and why different stabilisation mechanisms carry very different risks.
objectives: Explain fiat-backed, asset-referenced, crypto-collateralised and algorithmic designs
Analyse the revenue model and incentives of stablecoin issuers
Map the roles of issuers, reserve managers, custodians, distributors and wallet providers
syllabus: Single-currency and asset-referenced stablecoins
Crypto-collateralised and algorithmic models and their failures
Issuance, primary redemption and secondary market trading
Use cases: crypto trading, payments, remittances and settlement

modules.title: Regulating Stablecoins: Authorisation and Prudential Requirements
modules.summary: How regional crypto-asset regimes and international recommendations approach stablecoin issuers, from authorisation and governance to capital, liquidity, recovery and orderly redemption plans.
objectives: Explain the international standards for stablecoin arrangements
Compare regulatory approaches to single-currency and asset-referenced stablecoins
Assess an issuer's authorisation application against core requirements
syllabus: FSB high-level recommendations and the Basel Committee prudential treatment
Authorisation, governance, fit and proper and conflicts of interest
Own funds, liquidity, recovery and redemption plans
Enhanced requirements for significant or systemic stablecoins

modules.title: Reserve Assets, Redemption and Run Risk
modules.summary: How reserve composition, custody and redemption design determine whether a stablecoin holds its peg under stress, and what de-pegging episodes teach supervisors about testing resilience.
objectives: Assess reserve composition, segregation, custody and attestation
Evaluate redemption rights and their practical operation under stress
Analyse run dynamics and lessons from de-pegging episodes
syllabus: Eligible reserve assets, concentration and liquidity under stress
Segregation, bankruptcy remoteness and custody of reserves
Attestations versus audits: what reserve reports actually prove
Run risk compared with bank runs and money market fund runs

modules.title: Tokenised Deposits and Bank-Issued Digital Money
modules.summary: How banks are representing deposits on distributed ledgers, how tokenised deposits differ from stablecoins in legal and prudential terms, and the supervisory questions they raise.
objectives: Explain how tokenised deposits work and how they differ from stablecoins
Assess prudential, deposit protection and operational implications for banks
Evaluate interoperability between tokenised deposits of different banks
syllabus: Tokenised deposits as bank liabilities: legal and accounting treatment
Capital, liquidity and deposit insurance implications
Programmability, smart contracts and operational risk
Shared ledgers and settlement between banks

modules.title: Central Bank Digital Currencies: Retail and Wholesale
modules.summary: The motivations for retail and wholesale CBDCs, the main design choices central banks face, and the implications for privacy, intermediaries and the supervisory perimeter.
objectives: Explain the policy objectives behind retail and wholesale CBDCs
Analyse key design choices: architecture, holding limits, privacy and offline use
Assess the roles and supervision of intermediaries distributing a CBDC
syllabus: Retail CBDC: objectives, architecture and remuneration
Wholesale CBDC and settlement of tokenised assets
Privacy, data protection and holding limits
Intermediary roles: onboarding, wallets and customer service

modules.title: Payments, Monetary Sovereignty and Financial Stability
modules.summary: How digital money could reshape payment systems, bank funding and monetary transmission, including currency substitution risks for smaller and emerging economies.
objectives: Analyse the impact of digital money on bank deposits, funding and credit intermediation
Assess the application of the PFMI to systemic stablecoin arrangements
Evaluate currency substitution and monetary sovereignty risks
syllabus: Deposit outflows, disintermediation and fire-sale channels
Systemic stablecoin arrangements and the PFMI
Monetary policy transmission and currency substitution
Interconnections between stablecoins, crypto markets and traditional finance

modules.title: Financial Crime and Consumer Protection
modules.summary: The money laundering, sanctions evasion and fraud risks associated with digital money, and the consumer protection issues arising from disclosure, redemption and wallet custody.
objectives: Identify typologies of illicit use of stablecoins and other digital money
Apply FATF standards, including the travel rule, to digital money arrangements
Evaluate consumer disclosure, redemption and complaints arrangements
syllabus: Illicit finance typologies, unhosted wallets and peer-to-peer transfers
FATF standards, the travel rule and freezing capabilities
Blockchain analytics as a supervisory and compliance tool
Consumer disclosures, marketing and redemption at par

modules.title: Cross-Border Payments and Interoperability
modules.summary: How digital money is being used to improve cross-border payments, the risks of regulatory arbitrage and fragmentation, and the role of international cooperation and multi-currency platforms.
objectives: Explain the G20 objectives for faster, cheaper and more transparent cross-border payments
Assess interoperability and fragmentation risks across ledgers and jurisdictions
Evaluate cooperation arrangements for globally active stablecoin issuers
syllabus: The G20 cross-border payments roadmap and digital money
Multi-currency and multi-CBDC platform experiments
Regulatory arbitrage and offshore issuance of stablecoins
Supervisory colleges and cross-border information sharing

modules.title: Supervising Digital Money Issuers in Practice
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a practical supervisory approach for digital money issuers, from ongoing monitoring and stress testing to recovery, wind-down and the authority's policy stance.
objectives: Apply a supervisory assessment framework to a digital money issuer
Formulate a supervisory response to reserve or redemption pressure
Design priorities for the authority's digital money policy and supervision
syllabus: Ongoing monitoring: reserve data, redemption flows and on-chain indicators
Liquidity stress testing and recovery and wind-down planning
Coordination between supervisors, central banks and payment overseers
Workshop: supervisory response to a de-pegging scenario

related.title: Crypto and Blockchain Fundamentals
related.summary: A ten-module foundation programme giving supervisors a practical understanding of blockchain, crypto-asset markets and service providers, and the risks they must supervise.

related.title: Crypto-Asset Regulation and Supervision
related.summary: An advanced twelve-module programme equipping supervisors to authorise, supervise and take action against crypto-asset firms under comprehensive regimes and international standards.

related.title: MiCA Essentials for Supervisors (EU Edition)
related.summary: A six-module essentials programme giving EU national competent authority staff a practical command of MiCA, from token regimes and CASP authorisation to supervision and enforcement.

related.title: Supervising Crypto-Asset Service Providers under MiCA (EU Edition)
related.summary: An advanced fifteen-module programme equipping EU national competent authorities to authorise and supervise crypto-asset service providers and token issuers under MiCA.

related.title: Tokenisation of Financial Markets
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess tokenised securities, funds and collateral, DLT market infrastructure, settlement finality, custody and smart contract risk.

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.
